title: Attention Mechanism
subtitle: Module 8 · T1 Chapter 11 · encoder–decoder, the context bottleneck, query–key–value, scoring functions, Bahdanau attention, attention types and positional encoding

lesson.title: Encoder–decoder and its bottleneck
lesson.lead: Seq2seq splits **reading** (encoder) from **writing** (decoder), but squeezes the whole input into **one fixed vector c**.

blocks.text: Many tasks map a sequence of length T to one of a different length T′: question answering, summarisation, translation. A plain RNN gives one output per input, so it can't do that.
encoder: hₜᵉⁿᶜ = φ(W hₜ₋₁ + U xₜ + b),  c = h_Tᵉⁿᶜ     decoder: h₀ᵈᵉᶜ = c,  hₜᵈᵉᶜ = φ(W hₜ₋₁ + U yₜ₋₁ + b),  P(yₜ) = softmax(W_o hₜᵈᵉᶜ)

blocks.label: Key term
blocks.text: **Exposure bias:** the decoder is trained on perfect inputs but tested on its own (possibly wrong) outputs, so errors compound. Attention errors early in decoding feed wrong tokens into later steps.
The bottleneck

items: **Information loss:** long inputs → early tokens forgotten (performance drops past ~30 tokens, Sutskever 2014).
**Fixed capacity:** e.g. 512 numbers for any input length.
**No selectivity:** every part of the input is weighted equally.

lesson.title: The attention idea
lesson.lead: Give the decoder a **different context cₜ at every step**: a weighted average of all encoder states.

blocks.text: cₜ = Σᵢ αₜ,ᵢ hᵢ,    αₜ,ᵢ ≥ 0,    Σᵢ αₜ,ᵢ = 1
The weights α are learned from data and say where to look. Timeline: Seq2seq (2014, fixed context) → Bahdanau attention (2014, dynamic) → Transformer (2017, attention only).
Examples from the deck
Gold price, 7 days ₹6,200 … ₹6,300 with weights 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.15, 0.25, 0.23, 0.22 (recent days weigh more): c = Σαᵢxᵢ ≈ **₹6,261**.
Sentiment: in "quality is excellent but delivery was very slow" the model puts α = 0.35 on "excellent". QA: "What is the national capital?" puts 0.45 on "Delhi" and ignores "financial capital".

lesson.title: Query, key, value
lesson.lead: Attention is a **soft database lookup**: the query is compared with keys, and the matching values are retrieved.

lesson.title: Scoring functions
lesson.lead: Dot product is fast; **scaled** dot product is the Transformer default; additive handles different sizes.

blocks.text: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V
**Why scale?** For random vectors the dot product's variance grows with d_k. Big scores push softmax to one-hot, where its gradient is ≈ 0. Dividing by √d_k keeps the scores in a healthy range.

blocks.label: Slide check
blocks.text: The slide prints the weights as 0.21, 0.62, 0.17. Softmax of (0.58, 1.14, 0.44) is actually **(0.276, 0.484, 0.240)**. The ranking is the same, but compute it yourself in an exam.
Complexity: scaled dot product O(m·n·d) as one matrix product (very GPU-friendly); additive O(m·n·d·h).

lesson.title: Bahdanau attention
lesson.lead: The original (2014) attention for translation: **additive** scores between the previous decoder state and every encoder state.

items: Scores eₜ,ᵢ = vᵀ tanh(W_s sₜ₋₁ + W_h hᵢ).
Decoder update sₜ = RNN([yₜ₋₁; cₜ], sₜ₋₁).

blocks.text: The encoder is a **bidirectional RNN**, so hᵢ = [h→ᵢ; h←ᵢ] carries both past and future context.
Alignment: in yah kitaab bahut achchhi hai → This book is very good, the attention matrix is nearly diagonal (yah ↔ This 0.85, kitaab ↔ book 0.82).

head: Phase
Detail
rows: Teacher forcing; cross-entropy −Σ log P(y*ₜ); Adam with warmup; dropout
Greedy or beam search (k ≈ 5); a fresh cₜ every step; stop at ⟨END⟩

lesson.title: Types of attention
lesson.lead: The types differ in **where Q, K and V come from**, and what each position may see.

blocks.text: causal mask: Mᵢⱼ = 0 if j ≤ i, −∞ if j > i   (lower-triangular; −∞ becomes weight 0 after softmax)
MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head₁, …, head_h) W^O,   headᵢ = Attention(QWᵢ^Q, KWᵢ^K, VWᵢ^V)
blocks.caption: typical: h = 8, d_model = 512, d_k = d_v = 64

blocks.text: Example heads: one tracks syntax (verb → subject), one coreference ("he" → "customer"), one adjacent words ("very happy"). For gold prices: short-term, weekly and monthly patterns.

lesson.title: Self-attention vs CNN vs RNN
lesson.lead: Self-attention connects **any two positions in one step** but costs O(n²).

blocks.text: Q = XW^Q, K = XW^K, V = XW^V,   Z = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k) V ∈ R^{n×d_v}
Every output zᵢ is a weighted mix of **all** inputs. That's why Transformers train 10–100× faster than RNNs on long sequences.

lesson.title: Positional encoding
lesson.lead: Self-attention is **permutation-invariant**, so word order must be added to the embeddings.

blocks.text: Without positions, "Dog bites man" and "Man bites dog" look identical. The fix: x̃ᵢ = xᵢ + pᵢ.
PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d_model}),   PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d_model})

Example with d_model = 4: PE(0) = (0, 1, 0, 1); PE(1) = (0.841, 0.540, 0.010, 1.000); PE(2) = (0.909, −0.416, 0.020, 1.000). Low dimensions change fast (fine position), high dimensions change slowly (coarse position).

blocks.label: Key property
blocks.text: Why sinusoids work: sin(a + b) = sin a cos b + cos a sin b, so PE(pos + k) is a **linear function** of PE(pos). The model can learn relative offsets ("3 positions back").

worked.title: Context vector and its sensitivity (EC-3 2026 Q3)

problem.text: Encoder states h = (0.3, 0.5, 0.2); weights α = (0.2, 0.6, 0.2). (i) Compute cₜ. (ii) h₂ is perturbed to 0.1: recompute and quantify the change.

steps.label: Sensitivity
steps.text: ∂c/∂h₂ = α₂ = 0.6: the dominant weight passes 60% of any noise in h₂ straight into the context.

steps.label: Long sequences
steps.text: With many tokens, the weights spread thin (softmax dilution) or one token dominates; cost is O(n²) and attention weights aren't guaranteed explanations.

steps.label: Exposure bias
steps.text: Training uses ground-truth inputs, inference uses the model's own. An attention error causes a wrong token, which shifts the next query, which misaligns attention again: errors compound.

worked.answer: 0.40 → 0.16 (−0.24). Attention is most sensitive to the input with the largest weight.

worked.title: Dot-product attention weights (slide example)

problem.text: q = (0.8, 0.6); keys k₁ = (0.5, 0.3), k₂ = (0.9, 0.7), k₃ = (0.4, 0.2). Find the scores and weights.

worked.answer: α = (0.276, 0.484, 0.240). The slide's 0.21, 0.62, 0.17 is an arithmetic slip; key 2 wins either way.

worked.title: Scaled self-attention on 3 tokens

problem.text: X = rows (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1); take Q = K = X (identity projections), V = rows (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6), d_k = 2.

worked.answer: Each output row is a convex mix of the value rows. Check it in the Lab bench.

flashcards.front: Why does a plain RNN struggle with QA or summarisation?
flashcards.back: It gives one output per input step; the input and output lengths differ.
The whole input is squeezed into one fixed vector c: long inputs lose information.
Feed the ground-truth previous token to the decoder during training.
Trained on true tokens but tested on its own predictions, so errors compound.
cₜ = Σᵢ αₜ,ᵢ hᵢ, weights ≥ 0 summing to 1, recomputed every step.
Query: what I need. Keys: what can match. Values: what I retrieve.
Dot products grow with d_k → softmax saturates to one-hot → gradients ≈ 0.
vᵀ tanh(W_q q + W_k k); works when d_q ≠ d_k.
Self: Q, K, V from the same sequence. Cross: Q from the decoder, K and V from the encoder.
−∞ above the diagonal so token i only sees j ≤ i.
h parallel heads with their own projections, concatenated then × W^O.
Self-attention is permutation-invariant; word order must be injected.
Learned can't extrapolate past the training length; sinusoidal can.

formulas.name: Attention
formulas.formula: c = Σᵢ αᵢvᵢ,  αᵢ = softmax(score(q, kᵢ))

formulas.name: Bahdanau step
formulas.formula: eₜ,ᵢ = vᵀtanh(W_s sₜ₋₁ + W_h hᵢ); cₜ = Σ αₜ,ᵢ hᵢ; sₜ = RNN([yₜ₋₁; cₜ], sₜ₋₁)

formulas.name: Complexity
formulas.formula: Self-attention O(n²d) · RNN O(nd²) · CNN O(knd²)
